newsitem.title: UK: UK Tory stance on EMU likely to leave voters cold.
newsitem.headline: UK Tory stance on EMU likely to leave voters cold.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major's new harder line on Europe, announced to parliament on Thursday, will do little to win over sceptical British voters in the coming general election, political analysts said on Friday.
But if it quells Conservative in-fighting over the single currency and unites the government in the eyes of the electorate, Major may have scored a slight political advantage, they said.
"The direct effect on voting will be minuscule," said Ivor Crewe, vice chancellor and professor of government at the University of Essex.
"But there may be an indirect effect if this formula of "unlikely but not impossible" does the trick of uniting the party and keeping the dissidents quiet."

Major all but ruled out British participation in a European single currency in 1999 on Thursday, saying there was no chance of joining if other European Union states "fudged" the economic criteria for entry.
"It is very unlikely, though not impossible, that the single currency itself could proceed safely on January 1, 1999," he told parliament.

Political analysts said Europe would not be a major issue for Britons in the election, which must be held by May, especially as there is very little separating the two main political parties on the subject.
Both have said they would hold a referendum before taking Britain into a single currency. Labour appears slightly more sympathetic to the project but has avoided making any firm commitments.
"The electorate is terribly uninterested in Europe," said Ben Pimlott of Birkbeck College in London.
"I think Major's statement will make zero difference. I don't think voters are that switched into these statements by politicians."
Analysts said the government's new harder line on Europe did little to create any "clear blue water" between Labour and the Conservatives over Europe.
"It's not doing what Euro-sceptic members of the public, who haven't yet decided how to vote, are looking for," said Brian Gosschalk, managing director of polling company MORI.
"But equally it's not going to appeal to people who believe Britain should be playing a full part in Europe."
Opinion polls show around two-thirds of Britons oppose a single European currency, but around the same proportion are nevertheless in favour of staying in Europe.

In-fighting over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) within the Conservative party has been a recurring problem for the government, which faces an uphill battle to get re-elected. The Conservatives trail the opposition Labour party by around 20 points in the polls.
Birkbeck's Pimlott said there was a danger the latest government line on EMU could prompt even more dissent, rather than quash it as intended.
"I took the statement to be a small olive branch to the Euro-sceptics," he said.

"But the only question is whether that annoys the Euro-fanatics of the party sufficiently to make one of them speak out of turn, which would then draw attention to the divisions within the Conservative party."
Two British newspapers on Friday reported that up to 40 pro-European Conservative members of parliament were considering splitting from the ruling party.

The reports said the MPs were threatening to break away and back Labour over Europe if the Conservative leadership fell into the hands of "Euro-sceptic" Defence Secretary Michael Portillo after the election.
